 The Medicare mistakes even smart retirees make (and how to dodge them)
 AOL Staff 2026년 11월 6일 금 오후 4:58 UTC 0 Decoding Medicare Open Enrollment runs October 15 to December 7. A little homework now can save you serious money (and spare you a penalty that sticks around for life). 
 Turning 65 comes with some real perks. (Senior discounts! Fewer fashion rules!) Then the Medicare mail starts piling up, the phone starts ringing at dinnertime, and suddenly you're decoding Parts A, B, C and D like a pop quiz nobody warned you about.
 Here's the good news: most Medicare mistakes are totally avoidable once you know where people trip up. These are the nine that catch even the savviest planners off guard, plus how to sidestep every one.
 1. Snoozing on your sign-up window
 Your first chance to sign up is a seven-month window: the three months before your 65th birthday month, the birthday month itself, and the three months after. Miss it without other qualifying coverage, and your Part B premium jumps 10% for every full 12-month period you could have enrolled but didn't. And that surcharge? It's yours for life.
 What to do: Put the window on your calendar the year you turn 64. If you or your spouse are still working and covered by an employer with 20 or more employees, you can likely delay Part B. Ask HR to confirm, and keep proof of coverage so you can enroll penalty-free later.
 2. Skipping drug coverage because you feel fine
 Feeling healthy is a great reason to celebrate. It's a risky reason to skip drug coverage. Go 63 days or more without Part D or other "creditable" drug coverage (meaning coverage at least as good as Medicare's), and you'll owe a late penalty added to your premium for as long as you have Part D. Think of a low-cost plan now as a gift to future you.
 What to do: Enroll in a low-cost Part D plan or keep proof that your current coverage counts as creditable.
 3. Waiting for Medicare to come to you
 If you're already collecting Social Security when you turn 65, Medicare enrolls you in Parts A and B automatically. But plenty of people now hold off on claiming Social Security, and if that's you, Medicare won't come knocking. Nothing happens until you make the first move.
 What to do: If you aren't collecting Social Security yet, sign up yourself at ssa.gov or through your local Social Security office.
 4. Assuming your work insurance has your back
 Still working at 65? Good for you. Whether you can safely delay Medicare depends on the size of your employer. At companies with 20 or more employees, your work plan generally pays first, and the same goes if you’re covered through your spouse’s current job. At smaller companies, Medicare usually pays first, and your employer plan may cover very little if you never signed up. One more catch: if you contribute to a health savings account (HSA), you have to stop once you enroll in any part of Medicare.
 What to do: Ask your HR or benefits team one direct question: “Does our plan pay first or second once I’m eligible for Medicare?” Get the answer in writing. If you have an HSA, talk to a tax or benefits advisor before you enroll. Medicare Part A coverage can be backdated up to six months, so you’ll typically need to stop contributions earlier than you’d expect.

 Medicare Advantage and Part D plans can change their premiums, networks and covered drugs every single year. Each fall, your plan mails an Annual Notice of Change spelling out what’s different. It looks a lot like junk mail (and plenty of them land in the recycling bin unopened).
 What to do: Read the notice and compare it against your doctors and prescriptions. If something important changed, use Open Enrollment, which runs October 15 through December 7, to switch plans. Changes take effect January 1.
 6. Falling for the $0 premium
 A $0-premium plan sounds like a steal, until you add up the deductibles, copays and coinsurance. If you see specialists regularly or fill pricey prescriptions, a plan with a monthly premium can actually cost less over the full year. $0 doesn’t mean nothing: you’ll still pay your Part B premium.
 What to do: Estimate your total yearly cost: premium, plus deductible, plus what you'd expect to pay for your usual visits and drugs. Medicare's Plan Finder tool at medicare.gov does much of the math for you.
 7. Not checking that your doctors (and drugs) made the cut
 Medicare Advantage plans usually have networks, so the cardiologist you love may be in one plan and out of another. Part D and Advantage plans also have formularies (the list of drugs they cover), and where your drug lands on that list decides what you pay.
 What to do: Before you enroll, look up every doctor, hospital and pharmacy you rely on, plus every prescription, in the plan's directory and formulary. Call the doctor's office to double-check, since directories can be out of date.
 8. Letting the Medigap window slam shut
 If you go with Original Medicare, a Medigap (Medicare Supplement) policy can pick up many of the costs Medicare leaves behind. Your golden window to buy one is the six-month Medigap Open Enrollment Period that starts once you're 65 and enrolled in Part B. During those six months, insurers have to sell you a policy no matter your health. After that, in most states, they can charge you more or say no.
 What to do: Decide on Medigap early. If you think you might want it someday, the first six months are the time to get it.
 9. Assuming Medicare covers everything
 Medicare covers a lot. Not everything, though. Original Medicare doesn't pay for long-term care, like an extended nursing home stay or ongoing help at home, and it covers very little routine dental, vision or hearing care. So those cleanings, new glasses and hearing aids? Mostly on you.
 What to do: Make a list of what matters most to you, whether that's your teeth, your eyes or future care needs, and look for coverage that fills those gaps. That could be a Medicare Advantage plan with extra benefits, a standalone dental or vision policy, or long-term care planning.
 The bottom line
 You don't need to become a Medicare whiz overnight. You just need to know where the traps are, check your options every fall, and ask for help when the fine print gets fuzzy. So grab a cup of coffee, open that Annual Notice of Change, and circle December 7 on the calendar. Future you will be grateful.
